final_answer:
PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL - DRAFT REGULATORY APPROVAL MEMORANDUM
To: Executive Committee, CMB. Re: QuickBridge Lending, Inc. (QBL).
Basis: seven supplied documents (through April 14, 2025). Web access to primary law failed, so all legal statements are from counsel knowledge and NOT source-verified; cite-check and update before Whitfield & Crane review. Record premises (WA EWA Act, DFPI Interpretive Rule 2024-03, Oregon SB 1515, Colorado SB 21-196) are unverified.

1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
(a) No charter shortcut. Preemption belongs to the national bank, not its BHC affiliates. Under 12 U.S.C. 25b (Dodd-Frank 1044), as I recall it, state consumer financial laws apply to subsidiaries and affiliates of national banks, including operating subsidiaries, to the same extent as to any other entity. Cuomo v. Clearing House (2009) and Watters v. Wachovia (2007) predate it; 12 CFR 5.34 was conformed in 2011. Consequence: QBL needs state licenses in all eight states. The "alternative" of making QBL a CNB operating subsidiary under 5.34 probably does NOT deliver preemption either. This corrects the GC's premise and Clearwater Finding 1. Only CNB itself, lending in its own name (branch or division), gets 12 U.S.C. 85 and Barnett-type preemption, and that route carries true-lender, OCC, CRA and risk-concentration issues.
(b) Fed approval is probably not a pre-incorporation gating item. Reg Y 225.22(a) (verify) lets a qualifying BHC (well-capitalized and well-managed) enter de novo a 225.28 activity such as extending credit (225.28(b)(1)) without prior notice, with written notice to the Reserve Bank within about 10 business days after commencing the activity. Sections 225.23 (expedited notice) and 225.24 (application) govern acquisitions of going concerns or non-qualifying cases, so the GC's framing of "225.23-225.24" is probably the wrong track. Incorporating on June 15, 2025 is not "commencing" lending. Confirm CMB's BHC ratings (record gives only CNB's: composite 2, management Satisfactory, CRA Satisfactory) and that the open MRA does not impair "well-managed". Also file FR Y-10 for the new subsidiary (about 30 days). EWA fit under 225.28 depends on credit status (unresolved).
(c) Overstated BSA premise. The record (Chandrasekaran, Clearwater) assumes QBL is a BSA "financial institution" needing CIP, CDD, SAR and CTR. As I recall, FinCEN's "loan or finance company" definition (31 CFR 1010.100(lll)) reaches only residential mortgage lenders and originators and GSEs, so QBL's unsecured personal, business and EWA lending is likely not subject to a mandatory FinCEN AML program, CIP (bank rule, 31 CFR 1020.220) or CDD rule (1010.230, covered institutions only). No FinCEN registration category fits unless QBL does money transmission (it should not for its own advances; confirm). BUT: Reg Y 225.4(f) requires BHCs and nonbank subsidiaries to file SARs; OFAC applies to all US persons; Fed examiners expect enterprise-wide AML; and states may add requirements. Recommended: a risk-based program covering QBL (CMB-level, shared BSA Officer permitted, QBL-specific risk assessment), as a Fed expectation not a FinCEN mandate.
(d) EWA is a likely show-stopper: if the fee is a finance charge, APRs run 21% to 300%+ (section 3).
(e) Q1 2026 launch in eight states is unrealistic (section 7).

2. FEDERAL APPROVALS
Federal Reserve: above. Reg W/Sections 23A-23B: QBL is a CNB affiliate, so CNB's purchase of QBL participations is a covered transaction (10% per-affiliate / 20% aggregate capital limits, market terms). Neither the record nor Clearwater addresses this; map limits first.
OCC: no OCC approval for a CMB sub. OCC interest is indirect: CNB participations (above), shared services, and MRA follow-up (next OCC exam est. Q3 2025). An operating subsidiary needs a 5.34 filing, is limited to national-bank-permissible activities, and brings OCC supervision and CRA consequences.
FinCEN: see 1(c). MSB registration only if money transmission is found.
CFPB: Larger Participant Rule (12 CFR Part 1090) does not list general consumer installment or business lending (current categories as recalled: consumer reporting, debt collection, student loan servicing, international money transfer, auto financing, and a 2024 digital payments rule that I understand Congress disapproved in 2025; verify). Business lending is outside CFPB jurisdiction except ECOA. Exposures: 12 U.S.C. 5514(a)(1)(C) "reasonable cause" authority (12 CFR Part 1091), and 5514(a)(1)(E) payday-lender supervision regardless of size, which EWA treated as credit may trigger (unresolved). The FTC Safeguards Rule (16 CFR Part 314) applies to QBL; state regulators can enforce the CFPA (12 U.S.C. 5552). CFPB posture shifted in 2025; verify.

3. PRODUCTS
Personal loans (consumer credit): TILA/Reg Z closed-end disclosures; origination fee (up to 3%, withheld from proceeds) is a prepaid finance charge and enters the APR. The record's "7.99%-29.99% APR" must be the all-in Reg Z APR including that fee, or the pricing is misdescribed. Missed issues: (1) EFTA 15 U.S.C. 1693k / Reg E 1005.10(e): lender may not condition credit on repayment by preauthorized EFT; the term sheet's "ACH auto-debit" must be optional. (2) Military Lending Act: 36% MAPR including fees for covered borrowers; 29.99% plus a 3% fee can approach the cap on short terms. Compute before launch. (3) State caps: Oregon 36% all-in (record cites SB 1515; ORS ch. 725 license; verify). California: CFL tiered caps below $10,000 and administrative-fee limits (I recall roughly $75 for loans over $2,500), so a 3% fee on loans above $2,500 likely violates CFL; unconscionability exposure above $10,000 (verify). Colorado UCCC: verify. Arizona: Clearwater says no caps; I recall A.R.S. consumer-lender rate caps and a $10,000 loan ceiling for the license (verify). Texas: Clearwater says no usury cap; Finance Code ch. 342 sets tiered rate ceilings (verify). (4) Eligibility limited to citizens/permanent residents with SSNs invites 42 U.S.C. 1981 and state-law challenge though Reg B 1002.6(b)(7) permits immigration-status consideration.
Business line of credit: Reg Z does not apply (business purpose, 1026.3(a)); ECOA/Reg B does (notice rules vary at revenue of $1M; plan allows up to $5M). California CFL license covers commercial loans, and California commercial-financing disclosures (Fin. Code 22800 et seq.) apply to financing of $500,000 or less. Texas commercial usury ceilings (Finance Code ch. 303; I recall an 18% floor with a 24% cap, 28% above $250,000) could be exceeded by Prime+12.0% (about 19.5% at 7.50% Prime in March 2025) plus the 1.5% draw fee and $150 annual fee, since fees count. Clearwater's 8.50% Prime looks wrong (7.50% in March 2025; verify). FCRA: pulling owners' personal credit without liability or written consent may lack permissible purpose (guarantee required only above $100,000).
QuickBridge Advance (EWA): Record position: "not a loan." Federal treatment of fee-based EWA is unsettled (2020 advisory opinion, 2024 proposal later withdrawn per my recollection; verify). State: Nevada has an EWA licensing statute (recollection of 2023 legislation; verify; Nevada is a target state and the record is silent). Washington and California: record cites WA Act (eff. July 1, 2025) and DFPI Interpretive Rule 2024-03 as treating fee-based EWA as credit; I could not verify either. Fee looks less optional because QBL (not the employer) funds advances and two advances per period are allowed; no recourse, no credit check and no late fees help.
APR model (fee/advance x 365/days; single advance, single repayment, Reg Z actuarial result for one period): $100 repaid in 7 days: 3.99% x 52.14 = 208%. $100/14 days: 104%. $150/7 days: 139%. $250/7: 83%; $250/14: 42%. $500/7: 42%; $500/14: 21%. The 36% line requires advances of at least about $289 at 14 days, and none within the $500 cap at 7 days ($578 needed). Representative advance is $150 (term sheet), so Oregon's 36% cap and any other cap fail across the typical range if the fee is a finance charge. If treated as credit: TILA disclosures of $3.99 finance charge and APR on every advance; MLA 36% breach; state licensing. The revenue plan is also internally inconsistent: $1.5M/$3.99 = about 376,000 express transactions, but $25M volume at a $150 average implies about 167,000 advances (or a $66 average advance, producing APRs above 300% at 7 days). Recommendation: no EWA launch in CA, WA, NV, OR or CO without a written opinion; removing the fee is safest.

4. STATE LICENSING (record data from Clearwater Appendix C; statutes beyond that are unverified)
Oregon: DCBS consumer finance license, ORS ch. 725; 60-90 days. Washington: DFI, RCW 31.04; 60-90 days. California: DFPI CFL; 4-6+ months. Idaho: Idaho Credit Code lender license; 60-90 days. Nevada: NRS ch. 675 installment license, FID; 60-90 days (plus NRS 604A high-interest rules, EWA licensing). Arizona: DFI consumer lender license; 90-120 days. Colorado: UCCC supervised lender license; 60-90 days. Texas: OCCC, Fin. Code ch. 342 (or ch. 393 CAB); 90-120 days. All via NMLS (MU2/MU4 for control persons, financials, bonds, net worth; foreign qualification in each state). QBL can apply only after incorporation (NMLS 2-4 weeks, then sequential applications): realistic approvals are Oregon, Washington, Idaho, Nevada about Q1 2026 at best; California about Q2 2026 or later; Arizona and Texas Q1-Q2 2026. The plan's 60-90 days ignores deficiency cycles; a license is required before any loan.

5. VENDOR RISK, AI/ML, BSA, CONSUMER COMPLIANCE
Ridgeline MSA (executed Feb. 20, 2025 by CMB; assignable to QBL under 14.3 with CMB remaining jointly liable): no right-to-audit or regulator access (and confidentiality has no examiner carve-out); notice-only subcontractors (AWS GovCloud); no model access (IP provisions bar inspection/testing) and no ECOA warranty; breach terms limited to 72-hour notice with no consumer-notice, cost or fine indemnity; de-identified-data carve-out versus GLBA reuse limits; no regulatory termination right (270 days under change-in-law); liability cap about $2.4M versus $180M originations and regulator exposure; 5-year term, 6-month $1.2M convenience fee. Inconsistencies: the board resolution says renewals are "at CMB's election" but the MSA auto-renews absent 180 days' notice; Clearwater says no exit terms, but the MSA has 12-month paid transition assistance. Governance: the January resolution required a report-back before binding commitments, yet the MSA was signed and $250,000 paid before March ratification. OCC Bulletin 2013-29 and FIL-44-2008 (cited in the GC's request) were replaced by the June 2023 Interagency Guidance (OCC Bulletin 2023-17), which binds CNB and is persuasive for CMB/QBL.
AI/ML: ECOA/Reg B creditor liability for vendor models; specific adverse-action reasons (CFPB Circular 2022-03, 2023-03); SR 11-7 and OCC 2011-12 model risk (check whether revised since). Federal disparate-impact enforcement priorities shifted in 2025 (verify); state law and private suits remain.
BSA/AML and MRA: per section 1(c). Recommend an enterprise program with a QBL-specific risk assessment and a QBL compliance resource. The open MRA (moderate risk; plan submitted June 1, 2024; remediation scheduled Q3-Q4 2024; OCC acceptance still pending as of April 2025) is not a bar but is a supervisory risk; status update from Ms. Chandrasekaran still outstanding. The "April 2024" exam summary cites January 2025 events (date anomaly); confirm Clearwater's access complied with CSI limits (12 CFR Part 4).
Consumer: TILA/Reg Z, ECOA/Reg B (specific adverse-action reasons, CFPB Circulars 2022-03/2023-03), FCRA, UDAAP (12 U.S.C. 5531; avoid default-to-express design), GLBA/Reg P, state privacy laws (CA, CO, OR), EFTA, MLA, SCRA.

6. RISK RATING AND ACTIONS
Critical: (1) State licensing / no preemption (before incorporation: decide structure; budget eight licenses). (2) EWA classification and APR (before launch: opinion; redesign; exclude states). (3) Ridgeline MSA/model access (before launch: amendments incl. audit, model validation access, regulatory termination). (4) Timeline.
High: 23A/23B on participations; EFTA/MLA/fee compliance; fair lending validation; AML/SAR program and MRA closure; vendor program (CMB has none).
Medium: privacy/DPA; business-purpose usury; FCRA business pulls; eligibility criteria; CFPB readiness.
Before incorporation: Reg Y qualification, structure decision, board report-back. Before launch: licenses, MSA amendments, validation, AML program, privacy. Rolling: EWA law, CFPB changes.

7. TIMELINE
Q1 2026 launch in eight states is not feasible. Recommended: incorporate by June 15, 2025 (no Fed prior approval expected); file NMLS and apply in Oregon, Washington, Idaho, Nevada (personal loans, business LOC) in July-August 2025 rather than September, California first; launch phase 1 (four states, loans only) Q1 to Q2 2026 contingent on MSA amendment and model validation; phase 2 Arizona, Texas, California Q2 to Q3 2026; EWA deferred pending opinion and redesign. Currency: it is now October 2026; the record's dates have passed, so confirm actual incorporation, filing and license status and update.

Open: cite-check all law and the unverified state authorities; CMB ratings; MRA status.
